The HIV-1 genome is a single-stranded, positive sense, RNA molecule of approximately 9 kb in length.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the HIV genome is a complex mosaic of regions of high and low recombination propensity, and that the patterns of recombination in HIV-1 are influenced by selection acting both at the RNA and protein level.
the HIV genome is a complex, highly dynamic and highly recombination prone genetic entity, but that it is also highly structured, and this is likely to be a major factor influencing its evolution.
the HIV genome is a mosaic of functional units that have evolved to be recombination resistant and that the recombination hotspots are the inter-unit boundaries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selection has acted on HIV to ensure that genetic recombination occurs within a defined framework, and that this framework has evolved to minimise the impact that recombination has on viral fitness.
the genome structure of HIV has evolved in a way that minimises the deleterious effects of genetic recombination.
the genome architecture of the HIV-1M lineage is likely to be the result of an evolutionary arms race between the virus and host immune systems.
